title: Takeda's Narcolepsy Drug Orzeyful Hits US Market

contentHtml:
New Delhi: Takeda, said on Thursday its narcolepsy pill, the first treatment to target the underlying cause ​of the rare sleep disorder, is now available in the US after ‌a Drug Enforcement Administration decision removed the final regulatory hurdle for its rollout.

The DEA has classified Orzeyful as a Schedule IV controlled substance, the Japanese drugmaker said, a category considered to have a ​low potential for abuse and dependence. Schedule II drugs face stricter controls ​and Schedule V drugs the least.

The treatment is now available by prescription ⁠and will be dispensed through Cigna's Accredo Specialty Pharmacy, according to Takeda.

The US Food ​and Drug Administration had approved Orzeyful in August for narcolepsy type 1, a rare disorder ​caused by the loss of brain cells that produce orexin, a hormone that affects the brain's control over sleep and wake cycles.

Instead of just treating the symptoms, Orzeyful, a twice-daily pill, targets the loss ​of orexin signaling that causes the disorder, which is characterized by excessive daytime sleepiness, ​sudden loss of muscle tone, cognitive symptoms and disrupted nighttime sleep.

The US list price for Orzeyful ‌has been ⁠set at $16,500 per 60-tablet bottle, across all strengths. At least two analysts said this was below expectations, although in line with current standard-of-care therapies.

The pricing was "somewhat of a surprise" given the enhanced efficacy of the drug class, though the strategy could help expand ​patient access, said Truist ​analyst Alex Nackenoff.

About ⁠120,000 people in the US have the disorder, according to Takeda.

"Our initial launch efforts will be on adults who are cycling through ​other treatments or taking multiple medications and still experience breakthrough symptoms. ​And there ⁠is a broader opportunity given 50% of people with this rare disease are not even diagnosed," said Rhonda Pacheco, president of Takeda's US business unit.

In studies, the drug showed improvements ⁠in ​patients' ability to stay awake during the day compared ​with placebo, and significantly reduced instances of cataplexy, a sudden muscle weakness triggered by strong emotions.
